title: “I Didn’t Feel Like Getting Up To Train”: Casper Ruud Opens Up Ahead Of Paris Masters Clash With Alcaraz
text:

 Casper Ruud opened up about losing his motivation to train during a difficult period in 2025, explaining how professional help helped him regain his drive ahead of his Paris Masters semifinal against Carlos Alcaraz.
 by Sportscape Editor | Nov 07, 2026 | 2 minute read Casper Ruud discussed his mental health struggles, loss of motivation and recovery as he prepares to face Carlos Alcaraz in the Paris Masters semifinals. · Credits; Via ATP Tennis Casper Ruud has opened up about a difficult period in 2025 when he lost the desire to get up and train, explaining how mental health support helped him find his motivation again. Before facing Carlos Alcaraz in the Paris Masters semi-finals, the Norwegian spoke to Punto de Break about the pressure of life on the tennis tour, the tiring schedule and how he managed to overcome his struggles. Ruud has since returned to strong form and reached the last four in Paris, where he will face Alcaraz at 9:30 pm.
 Ruud Explains Why He Lost His Motivation to Train
 Ruud explained that life as a professional tennis player can become difficult because the daily routine rarely changes. Players spend hours training, travel from one country to another and compete in many tournaments. Although matches can be exciting, they also take a lot of mental energy. He said the busy schedule leaves little time for players to work on improving their game.
 “Last year, I had some mental problems, I wasn’t feeling well psychologically.
 But I sought help, it worked, and I got a quick response. I started to feel much better, so it really helped to have someone to talk to about certain things.
 I think the hardest thing is that it’s a very monotonous and repetitive life. We train for hours, whether in Miami, at Wimbledon, or anywhere else. It’s always the same. Training can be enjoyable, but also exhausting.
 Matches are exciting, of course, but they also represent a huge expenditure of mental energy.
 We have so many mandatory tournaments that it prevents us from enjoying long training periods, which are precisely the ones that allow you to truly improve.”
 He also explained how the lack of time to train properly affected his feelings about tennis. The long travel schedule and pressure to keep competing eventually made him lose the excitement he once had for practice.
 “When you play so many tournaments, it’s hard to find time to improve as a tennis player. Training becomes very repetitive and you end up wondering whether you can still improve, how to become a better player.
 It’s complicated because you don’t have time to breathe, to go home for a month or two and really train, working on specific aspects of your game.
 The only time you can do that is during the break between seasons. And yet, if you play the ATP Finals, you finish at the end of November and you have to be ready to start in Australia in early January.
 All of this brought me to a point last year where I no longer wanted to get up to go to training when the alarm went off in the morning.
 Until then, I had always trained because I wanted to. During that period, however, I did it because I had to.”
 Professional Help Helped Ruud Find His Love for Tennis Again
 Ruud said constant travelling, packing and unpacking, and catching flights had also become too much during that difficult period. He did not want to complain because he understood that many people have repetitive jobs, but he admitted that the routine had affected him. Seeking professional help and learning ways to manage those feelings helped him move forward.
 “I don’t want to complain, because I know many people have repetitive tasks, but you are constantly packing and unpacking your bags, going from one airport to another, catching flights and organizing your travel... Sometimes, all of that becomes too much of a burden. That’s what I felt last year.
 I did everything I could to get out of that state, and this season, things are going much better.
 I realized that my career wouldn’t last forever and that I had to try to enjoy the years I have left on the tour. But yes, it’s sometimes hard to overcome certain situations.
 Few people love their job every day of the year, but it was the first time I needed to turn off my alarm in the morning. I was training because it was my job, not because I wanted to improve.
 I was afraid to feel that way. It wasn’t pleasant. I sought help and tried to manage the situation as best I could.
 We found a solution as well as several techniques I can use if that feeling ever overwhelms me again. But I hope it won’t happen again.”
 Ruud also spoke warmly about Alcaraz, his upcoming opponent in Paris. He admitted that the Spaniard has beaten him in several important matches but said he respects him and enjoys competing against him. He also explained that time away from tennis during the summer, between his wedding and the grass-court season, helped him return with less physical and mental tiredness.
 “We have played great matches, most of which he won. The truth is, he has been my nemesis in some of the biggest matches of my career and he has taught me several valuable lessons.
 He’s a wonderful person, someone it’s always a pleasure to play against, and I’m looking forward to facing him.
 Honestly, I feel very good physically and I’ve been playing good tennis for a few weeks.
 I think the few weeks of rest I took this summer, between my wedding and the grass season, allowed me to approach this period with less physical and mental fatigue than usual.
 I’m playing good tennis and I hope I can keep it up against Carlos.”
 After overcoming a difficult period and finding his enjoyment of tennis again, Ruud now has a chance to reach the Paris Masters final. His words also show why taking care of mental well-being and finding time to rest can be important for a long tennis career.
